title: Economic Bulletin Issue 2, 2026
summary: The ECB Governing Council kept interest rates unchanged at its 19 March 2026 meeting, citing significant uncertainty from the war in the Middle East creating upside inflation risks and downside growth risks. ECB staff revised up their inflation projections to 2.6% for 2026 (vs prior path) and revised down GDP growth to 0.9% for 2026, reflecting higher energy prices and disruptions to commodity markets, real incomes and confidence.
key_points: ECB kept three key interest rates unchanged on 19 March 2026, maintaining its data-dependent approach without pre-committing to a specific rate path
Staff revised headline inflation projections to 2.6% in 2026, 2.0% in 2027, and 2.1% in 2028, up from the December 2025 projections due to higher energy prices from the Middle East war
GDP growth projections revised down to 0.9% in 2026 (-0.3pp vs December), 1.3% in 2027 (-0.1pp), and 1.4% in 2028 (unchanged)
Euro area annual HICP inflation rose to 1.9% in February 2026 from 1.7% in January; core inflation (excluding energy and food) increased to 2.4% from 2.2%
Alternative scenarios suggest a prolonged oil and gas supply disruption would push inflation above baseline and growth below baseline; second-round effects on medium-term inflation remain uncertain
Q4 2025 GDP grew 0.2% quarter-on-quarter, driven by stronger domestic demand, with consumption supported by rising real incomes and low unemployment
why_it_matters: The ECB's decision to hold rates steady while raising its inflation forecast signals a delicate balancing act between energy-driven price pressures and weakening growth. The Middle East conflict has emerged as a key macro catalyst requiring close monitoring. Markets should watch for the ECB's next data-dependent moves as energy price trajectories and second-round inflation effects become clearer over the coming months.
macro_context: The war in the Middle East represents a major macro catalyst with dual effects: higher energy prices pushing inflation above target while simultaneously weighing on growth through disrupted commodity markets, reduced real incomes, and diminished consumer confidence. The ECB's projections are conditioned on futures market energy prices as of 11 March 2026. Alternative scenarios explore a prolonged energy shock with more severe growth downside. Longer-term inflation expectations remain well anchored at around 2%, and the Governing Council emphasized its determination to maintain price stability. The euro area's structural competitiveness challenges persist alongside geopolitical risks.
important_numbers: 1.9% - Euro area HICP inflation in February 2026
notes: Source is a primary ECB publication (Economic Bulletin) from the same week as the rate decision, containing both the policy decision and staff macroeconomic projections.
